read.passage: In 1912, as Robert Falcon Scott's team struggled back from the South Pole, Captain Lawrence Oates, weak and frostbitten, stepped out of the tent into a blizzard with the words, 'I am just going outside and may be some time.' He was never seen again. The line has become a famous example of understatement: by saying far less than he meant, Oates conveyed courage without drama. Linguists note that such indirectness works only when speaker and listener share assumptions. Among close colleagues, 'You might want to look at this again' is understood as a clear instruction; to a newcomer from a more direct culture, it may sound like an optional suggestion. Skilled communicators therefore adjust: they keep the courtesy of indirect speech but check, discreetly, that the message has landed.

qs.q: Why is Oates's line considered an understatement?
options: He described a fatal decision in very mild words.
He exaggerated the danger of the storm.
He refused to explain his plan.

qs.q: According to the passage, indirectness works only when …
options: the listener is older than the speaker

qs.q: How might a newcomer misunderstand 'You might want to look at this again'?
What do skilled communicators do, according to the passage?
options: Stay polite but check that the message was understood
Always speak as directly as possible
